samples.text:
Nowadays, many students bring their mobile phones to school and they are often distracted by them during the lessons. This essay will discuss the main problems of this situation and suggest some solutions to solve them.

The first problem is that students cannot concentrate on what teacher is saying. When a phone vibrates or they receive a message, they want to check it immediately, so they miss important informations. As a result, their marks in exams can become lower. Another problem is that it disturb other students in the class. For example, if one student is watching videos or playing games, the students who sit next to him will also look at the screen and stop listening. Also, teachers have to stop the lesson many times to tell students to put away phones, and this waste a lot of time.

However, there are some solutions for these problems. Firstly, schools can make a clear rule that phones are not allowed during lessons. Students could leave their phones in a box at the start of the class and take them back at the end of the day. Secondly, parents should also help. They can talk to their children about the dangers of using phone too much and explain why it is important to focus in school. Finally, teachers can make lessons more interesting, because when the lesson is boring, students are more likely to use their phones.

In conclusion, mobile phones cause many problems in the classroom, such as poor concentration and wasting of time. I think schools, parents and teachers should work together to solve this problem, and if they do this, students will be more focus on their studies.
samples.why: Both parts addressed with relevant ideas · examples are simple and some points underdeveloped · mechanical linking (Firstly, Secondly, Also) · adequate vocabulary · several agreement, article and word-form errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
Mobile phones have become a constant presence in the lives of teenagers, and it is now common for students to be distracted by them even in the middle of a lesson. This habit creates difficulties for both learners and teachers, but I believe it can be managed through a combination of school policy and better classroom practice.

The most obvious problem is the damage to students' learning. Checking a notification may take only a few seconds, but each interruption breaks a student's concentration, and it can take several minutes to fully refocus on a difficult explanation. Over time, pupils who are frequently distracted tend to develop gaps in their understanding, which is often reflected in lower exam results. A second issue concerns the class as a whole. When teachers have to repeatedly ask students to put their phones away, valuable teaching time is lost and the atmosphere of the lesson can become tense. In addition, a student secretly watching videos can easily distract the classmates sitting around them.

There are, however, practical ways of tackling these problems. The most effective is probably a clear and consistently enforced policy, such as requiring students to hand in their phones at the start of the day or keep them switched off in lockers. Such rules only work if every teacher applies them, otherwise students quickly learn in which lessons they can ignore them. At the same time, schools could teach pupils about healthy technology habits, so that they understand why constant phone use harms their attention. Teachers can also reduce the temptation by designing more interactive lessons, since students who are actively involved are less likely to reach for their phones.

In conclusion, phone use during lessons weakens concentration and wastes valuable teaching time. Firm school rules, supported by education about digital habits and engaging teaching, offer the best chance of solving the problem.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · problems and solutions extended with explanation · clear topic in each paragraph · range of linking with minor punctuation slips · good collocation (consistently enforced policy) · mostly error-free complex sentences.

samples.text:
In classrooms across the world, the smartphone has become a persistent rival for students' attention. While the device itself is not inherently harmful, its presence during lessons undermines both individual learning and the functioning of the class, and addressing this requires action from schools, teachers and families alike.

The most serious consequence is the erosion of sustained concentration. Learning complex material, whether an algebraic proof or the causes of a historical conflict, depends on following a line of reasoning without interruption. A single glance at a message may seem trivial, yet it fractures that reasoning, and a student who is interrupted repeatedly is left with a fragmented grasp of the topic that later surfaces as poor performance in assessments. Beyond the individual, phones damage the shared environment of the classroom. Teachers forced to police screen use lose time that should be spent teaching, and the constant tension between enforcement and instruction can sour relationships between staff and pupils. Moreover, distraction is contagious: one student scrolling through videos can draw the attention of an entire row.

The most direct remedy is an unambiguous, school-wide policy. Requiring phones to be stored in lockers or sealed pouches during the school day removes the temptation altogether, and applying the rule uniformly prevents the inconsistency that students are quick to exploit. However, restriction alone treats the symptom rather than the cause. Schools should also build digital literacy into the curriculum, helping young people understand how apps are designed to capture attention and how to regain control over their own habits. Parents have a complementary role in reinforcing these messages at home, while teachers can reduce the appeal of the phone by making lessons more participatory and less reliant on passive listening.

In short, mobile phones weaken concentration, waste teaching time and strain classroom relationships. A consistent ban, combined with education that equips students to manage technology themselves, offers the most durable solution.
samples.why: Both parts fully developed with extended, well-supported ideas · logical sequencing and well-managed paragraphing · precise, flexible vocabulary (erosion, fractures, complementary role) · wide range of structures, virtually error-free.
